title: "Dates and Times"
unit: 2
cluster: "Cookbook"

Programs often need to work with dates and times, such as when a train departs
or how long a journey takes. Python's `datetime` module has types that
represent a date and time, and the difference between two of them.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to:

* create a `datetime` value
* read the parts of a `datetime` and compare two of them
* find the time difference between two `datetime` values
* print a date and time in the form we want

## Creating a date and time

The `datetime` module has a type that is also named `datetime`. A `datetime`
value holds a date and a time of day.

Calling the type with the year, month, day, hour and minute creates a
`datetime`:

```{python}
import datetime

datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 20, 17, 0)
```

The `now()` function creates a `datetime` with the current date and time:

```{python}
datetime.datetime.now()
```

Dates and times often arrive as strings, such as `"2026-10-20 17:00"`. The
`fromisoformat()` function converts a string like this into a `datetime`:

```{python}
datetime.datetime.fromisoformat("2026-10-20 17:00")
```

The string has the year, month and day, then the hours and minutes. The
seconds can be included too:

```{python}
datetime.datetime.fromisoformat("2026-10-20 17:00:30")
```

The parts must be in this order, with these separators. A string in another
form raises an error:

```python
datetime.datetime.fromisoformat("20-10-2026")
```

```text
ValueError: Invalid isoformat string: '20-10-2026'
```

## Operations on a datetime

Each part of a `datetime` is available as an attribute: `year`, `month`,
`day`, `hour` and `minute`.

```{python}
departure = datetime.datetime.fromisoformat("2026-10-20 17:00")
departure.year
```

```{python}
departure.hour
```

Two `datetime` values can be compared. An earlier time is less than a later
one:

```{python}
arrival = datetime.datetime.fromisoformat("2026-10-21 08:32")
departure < arrival
```

Two `datetime` values are equal when they hold the same date and time, however
they were created:

```{python}
departure == datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 20, 17, 0)
```

## Time difference

Subtracting one `datetime` from another gives the time difference between
them:

```{python}
departure = datetime.datetime.fromisoformat("2026-10-20 17:00")
arrival = datetime.datetime.fromisoformat("2026-10-21 08:32")
duration = arrival - departure
duration
```

The result is not a `datetime`, but a value of another type, `timedelta`.
Python displays it in seconds. `print()` displays it in hours, minutes and
seconds:

```{python}
print(duration)
```

The journey takes 15 hours and 32 minutes. A `timedelta` longer than a day is
printed with the number of days first:

```{python}
departure = datetime.datetime.fromisoformat("2026-10-20 19:20")
arrival = datetime.datetime.fromisoformat("2026-10-22 06:40")
print(arrival - departure)
```

The `total_seconds()` method gives the whole duration in seconds, which can be
converted into other units:

```{python}
duration = arrival - departure
duration.total_seconds() / 60
```

The journey takes 2120 minutes.

## Printing a date and time

`print()` displays a `datetime` with the date first, then the time:

```{python}
departure = datetime.datetime.fromisoformat("2026-10-20 17:00")
print(departure)
```

The `isoformat()` method converts a `datetime` into a string in the same form
that `fromisoformat()` reads. A `T` separates the date from the time:

```{python}
departure.isoformat()
```

To have a space instead of the `T` between the date and the time, pass
`sep=" "` as an argument:

```{python}
departure.isoformat(sep=" ")
```

The `strftime()` method converts a `datetime` into a string in the form we
want. Its argument is a pattern. Each code that starts with `%` is replaced by
a part of the date or time, and the other characters stay as they are:

```{python}
print(departure.strftime("%d %b %Y"))
```

```{python}
print(departure.strftime("%a %d %b, %H:%M"))
```

These are the codes used most often:

| Code | Meaning | Example |
|------|---------|---------|
| `%Y` | year | `2026` |
| `%m` | month as a number | `10` |
| `%b` | short month name | `Oct` |
| `%d` | day of the month | `20` |
| `%a` | short weekday name | `Tue` |
| `%H` | hour, from `00` to `23` | `17` |
| `%M` | minute | `00` |

## Practice

### Problem 1

A train departs at `"2026-10-20 23:45"` and arrives at `"2026-10-22 05:15"`.
Print the duration of the journey.

The expected output is:

```text
1 day, 5:30:00
```

### Problem 2

Complete this program so that it prints the number of hours from the
departure to the arrival:

```python
import datetime

departure = "2026-10-20 06:00"
arrival = "2026-10-20 13:30"

# TODO: convert the two strings and print the hours between them
```

The expected output is:

```text
7.5
```

## Summary

A `datetime` holds a date and a time of day. Subtracting two of them gives a
`timedelta`, and `strftime()` converts a `datetime` into a string in a chosen
form.

| Form or rule | Meaning |
|--------------|---------|
| `datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 20, 17, 0)` | creates a `datetime` from the year, month, day, hour and minute |
| `datetime.datetime.now()` | creates a `datetime` with the current date and time |
| `datetime.datetime.fromisoformat("2026-10-20 17:00")` | converts the string into a `datetime` |
| `"2026-10-20 17:00"` or `"2026-10-20 17:00:30"` | the form `fromisoformat()` expects: year, month, day, then the time |
| a string in another form | raises a `ValueError` |
| `departure.year`, `departure.hour` | a part of a `datetime` |
| `departure < arrival` | `True` if `departure` is earlier than `arrival` |
| `arrival - departure` | the time between two `datetime` values, as a `timedelta` |
| `print(departure)` | prints a `datetime` as `2026-10-20 17:00:00` |
| `departure.isoformat()` | converts a `datetime` into a string such as `"2026-10-20T17:00:00"` |
| `departure.isoformat(sep=" ")` | the same, with a space instead of the `T`, such as `"2026-10-20 17:00:00"` |
| `print(duration)` | prints a `timedelta` as hours, minutes and seconds, with days first if any |
| `duration.total_seconds()` | the whole duration in seconds |
| `departure.strftime("%d %b %Y")` | converts a `datetime` into a string, such as `"20 Oct 2026"` |
